segments.translit: jñānānandapramodayukto hi siddhācāryyo bhadrapādas tam evārthaṃ pratipādayati—
segments.translation: For the [siddha]{siddha} master [Bhadrapāda]{p-bhadra}, endowed with delight in the [joy]{ananda} of [knowledge]{jnana}, sets forth that same point:
segments.note: Munidatta introduces the poet as the [siddha]{siddha} ('accomplished one') master [Bhadrapāda]{p-bhadra}, endowed with delight in the [joy]{ananda} of [knowledge]{jnana}, who sets forth 'that same point' (cp.35.m1). The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has him 'fully satisfied' (rab tu tshim pa) by the joy of knowledge.

flags.note: For pramoda ('delight') the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has rab tu tshim pa ('fully satisfied'): ye shes kyi dga' bas rab tu tshim pa dang ldan pa, 'endowed with full satisfaction through the joy of knowledge'. The sense is close; I translate the Sanskrit.

'That same point' (tam evārtham) has no antecedent inside this segment. In Munidatta's opening formula (cp.35.m1) it presumably points back to the theme he has just been expounding (the comment on song 34, not in this pack); it could also look forward to what Bhadrapāda goes on to say. I keep the phrase as it stands.

segments.translit: eta kāletyādi| anādisaṃsāre kalyāṇamitrasaṃsargāt| moham iti bāhyaviṣayasaṅgenā[na]lpakalpānta[ṃ] tāvat sthito 'smi| idānīṃ buddhānubhāvāt sadgurubodhaprasaṅgena mayā cittasya svarūpam avagatam|
segments.translation: 'For so long a time', and so on: in beginningless [saṃsāra]{samsara}, from association with a [spiritual friend]{kalyanamitra}. '[Delusion]{moha}' means: through attachment to external [sense objects]{visaya} I remained that long, for many aeons. Now, through the power of the [buddhas]{buddha}, by way of contact with the true [guru]{guru}'s teaching, I have understood the [true nature]{svarupa} of [mind]{citta}.
segments.note: Munidatta glosses 'so long a time' as beginningless [saṃsāra]{samsara} and the poet's [delusion]{moha} as attachment to external [sense objects]{visaya}, which held him for many aeons; now, by the buddhas' power and the true [guru]{guru}'s teaching, he has understood the [true nature]{svarupa} of [mind]{citta} (cp.35.m2). The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) says instead that his mind's nature 'becomes suchness'.

flags.note: kalyāṇamitrasaṃsargāt, 'from association with a spiritual friend', sits oddly in a gloss on the poet's long delusion. Three ways out: (1) the phrase is a compressed paraphrase of 1b given in advance ('in beginningless saṃsāra' for 1a, 'from association with a spiritual friend' for 1b), before the fuller glosses that follow; (2) read kalyāṇamitrāsaṃsargāt, 'for lack of association' (one vowel stroke more in the script); (3) read ā kalyāṇamitrasaṃsargāt, 'until association'. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) agrees with the printed text (dge ba'i bshes gnyen dang phrad pa las, 'from meeting a spiritual friend'), so the reading is old. I translate as printed and lean to (1).

For mayā cittasya svarūpam avagatam ('I have understood the true nature of mind') the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has bdag gi sems kyi rang bzhin de kho na nyid du 'gyur ro ('the nature of my mind becomes suchness'), and for sadgurubodhaprasaṅgena ('by way of contact with the true guru's teaching') only bla ma dam pa dang phrad pas ('through meeting the true guru'), with no word for bodha. Its sangs rgyas kyis mthus is presumably for sangs rgyas kyi mthus, 'by the power of the buddhas'.

[na] and [ṃ] in analpakalpāntaṃ are Shastri's restorations; the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293)'s dpag tu med pa'i bskal par ('for immeasurable aeons') supports them. I render analpakalpāntam ('to the end of not a few aeons') as 'for many aeons'.

segments.translit:
dhruvapadena tam evārthaṃ draḍhayati—
ebem̐m ityādi idānīṃ pavipadmasaṃyogākṣarasukhe cittarājo mama vinaṣṭagamanam iti prakṛtiprabhāsvare praviṣṭam iti|
segments.translation: With the [refrain]{dhruvapada} he makes that same point firm. 'Now', and so on: now, in the [imperishable bliss]{aksara-sukha} of the union of [vajra]{vajra} and [lotus]{lotus}, my [king of mind]{king-of-mind}, its going destroyed, has entered natural [clear light]{prabhasvara}.
segments.note: Munidatta takes the [refrain]{dhruvapada} as confirming the first couplet: in the [imperishable bliss]{aksara-sukha} of the union of [vajra]{vajra} and [lotus]{lotus}, the [king of mind]{king-of-mind}, its going destroyed, has entered natural [clear light]{prabhasvara}, which he puts where the song has the [sky-ocean]{gagana-samudra} (cp.35.m3). The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) says the king of mind 'became nonexistent' (med par gyur).

flags.note: For vinaṣṭagamanam ('its going destroyed') the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has med par gyur ('became nonexistent'), and it makes the bliss instrumental (mi 'gyur ba'i bde bas, 'through the unchanging bliss') where the Sanskrit has the locative akṣarasukhe ('in the imperishable bliss'). Otherwise it agrees, including rang bzhin gyis 'od gsal la rab tu zhugs ('fully entered natural clear light').

vinaṣṭagamanam and praviṣṭam are neuter beside the masculine cittarājaḥ, a looseness common in this commentary. I take vinaṣṭagamanam as 'whose going is destroyed', glossing ṇaṭhā ('perished', 2a); gamana ('going') may also pick up ṭaliā ('tottering', 2b). Munidatta paraphrases gaṇasamude with prakṛtiprabhāsvare (cp.35.m3) but gives no explicit 'X iti Y' gloss, so I record no equation. The machine transliteration's draṛhayati is draḍhayati.

segments.translit:
dvitīyapadenābhyāsasvarūpam āha—
pekhamītyādi| sarvvadharmmānupalaṃbhayogena yaṃ yaṃ digbhāgaṃ paśyāmi taṃ taṃ sarvvaśūnyaṃ prabhāsvaramayaṃ pratibhāti ataeva cittasyānudayena pāpapuṇyādikaṃ saṃsārabandhanañ ca jānāmīti|
tathā ca sarahapādāḥ—
aṅgem̐ pacchem ityādi|
segments.translation: With the second [verse]{pada} he states the [true nature]{svarupa} of [practice]{abhyasa}. 'I look', and so on: through the yoga of the [non-apprehension]{anupalambha} of all [dharmas]{dharma}, whatever direction I look in, all of it appears as [emptiness]{sunyata}, made of [clear light]{prabhasvara}. Therefore, through the non-arising of [mind]{citta}, I know [sin and merit]{papa-punya} and the like, and the [bond]{bandhana} of [saṃsāra]{samsara}. And so [Saraha]{p-saraha} says: 'In front and behind', and so on.
segments.note: Munidatta reads couplet 3, his second [verse]{pada}, as the nature of [practice]{abhyasa}: through the yoga of [non-apprehension]{anupalambha}, every direction appears as [emptiness]{sunyata} made of [clear light]{prabhasvara}, and through the non-arising of [mind]{citta} the poet knows [sin and merit]{papa-punya} and the [bond]{bandhana} of [saṃsāra]{samsara} (cp.35.m4). For 'non-arising of mind' the Tibetan has 'dawning of the fourth'.

citations.quoted: aṅgem̐ pacchem̐ ityādi: 'In front and behind', and so on (incipit only)
citations.work: Saraha, a dohā, presumably from his Dohākoṣa; Munidatta names only Saraha

flags.note: For cittasyānudayena ('through the non-arising of mind') the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has bzhi pa shar bas ('through the dawning of the fourth'), as if its manuscript read something like caturthasyodayena, the fourth presumably being the fourth joy that Munidatta names in cp.35.m5. The two differ in word and in polarity (non-arising against arising); udaya ('rising', shar ba) is common to both. The song's cia bihunne ('with the mind gone', 3b) supports the Sanskrit, which I translate.

pāpapuṇyādikaṃ saṃsārabandhanañ ca jānāmi: I translate 'I know sin and merit and the like, and the bond of saṃsāra'. It can also be read 'I know sin, merit and the like to be the bond of saṃsāra', and the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) takes it so (sdig pa dang bsod nams la sogs pas kyang 'khor bar 'ching bar bdag gis shes pa, 'I know that sin, merit and the rest also bind one in saṃsāra'). After the song's 'no sin and merit' one might expect 'I do not know', but neither witness has a negative.

aṅgem̐ in Saraha's incipit is probably for aggem̐ ('in front, before', Sanskrit agre): the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has sngon dang phyi ma, 'before and after'. I translate 'In front and behind', which suits the directions of 3a; 'Before and after' is the alternative. Only the opening words are quoted, so the dohā itself is not translated.
The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) adds bdag la so sor ('to me, each one') to 'appears' (pratibhāti), which suits the prefix prati-; no difference of sense.

segments.translit:
tṛtīyapadena vajraprabhāvam āha—
bājuletyādi| [52]vajrakuleneti| vajraguruṇā lakṣyam iti bhāvyam uktaṃ mahyaṃ caturthānandopāyaṃ pradattaṃ| mayā punaḥ sādaranirantarābhyāsena| gaganeti prabhāsvarasamudre ahārīkṛtam|
segments.translation: With the third [verse]{pada} he states the [power]{prabhava} of the [vajra]{vajra}. 'Bājule', and so on: 'by the [vajrakula]{vajrakula}' means by the [vajra]{vajra} [guru]{guru}. 'The [mark]{laksya}' means what is to be meditated on: it was spoken, and the [means]{upaya} of the fourth [joy]{ananda} was given to me. And I in turn, through devoted, unbroken [practice]{abhyasa}, lost it; '[sky]{gagana}' means: in the [ocean]{ocean} of [clear light]{prabhasvara}.
segments.note: Munidatta reads couplet 4, his third [verse]{pada}, as the [vajra]{vajra}'s [power]{prabhava}: bājule, 'by the [vajrakula]{vajrakula}' ('vajra family'), means by the vajra [guru]{guru}, who spoke the [mark]{laksya}, what is to be meditated on, and gave the poet the [means]{upaya} of the fourth [joy]{ananda}; through unbroken [practice]{abhyasa} the poet lost it in the [sky]{gagana}, the ocean of [clear light]{prabhasvara} (cp.35.m5).

equations.en: what is to be meditated on (bhāvya), the means of the fourth joy
in the ocean of clear light

flags.note: Who gives the mark in 4a. Munidatta's Sanskrit (cp.35.m5) has no personal name: he renders bājule with the instrumental vajrakulena and explains it, in his usual 'X iti Y' form, as vajraguruṇā, 'by the vajra guru' (Shastri's daṇḍa between them is like the one in 'abhāga iti| anutpāda...', cp.35.m6). So for him the agent of 4a is the vajra guru, called 'vajrakula'. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) cites the lemma as rA hu la (Rāhula), as in its verse line, yet glosses it rdo rje'i rigs la ('to/in the vajra family', dative-locative rather than agent) and goes on with rdo rje bla mas ('by the vajra guru'): its translators kept Munidatta's gloss while reading the lemma as a name. bājula may be a Prakrit form of vajrakula (vajja-ula, with the k of kula lost), which would support Munidatta; this is my suggestion.

For lakṣyam iti bhāvyam uktaṃ ('"the mark" means what is to be meditated on; it was spoken') the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has rdo rje bla mas mtshon nas dngos po las grol nas ('the vajra guru, having indicated, freed from things'): it takes lakṣ- as a verb, 'indicate', with the guru as subject, and reads bhāva-mukta, 'freed from things' (dngos po = bhāva), where the Sanskrit divides bhāvyam uktam. The unspaced script allows a different division, but bhāva for bhāvya needs a letter fewer. The Tibetan also lacks 'to me' (mahyam).

For ahārīkṛtam, the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293)'s comment has 'od gsal gyi rgya mtshor ster bar byas pa ('given into the ocean of clear light'), where its verse line 4b has stor bar gyur ('was lost'). ster and stor differ by one vowel sign, so ster is probably a slip for stor; either way the Tibetan offers nothing for 'ate'. Its introduction also reads rdo rje bla ma'i mthu ('the power of the vajra guru') for vajraprabhāvam ('the power of the vajra').

ahārīkṛtam is an -ī-kṛta formation ('made into X') on ahāra, the song's own word (ahārila 4b, ahāra kaelā 5b). As Sanskrit it would most naturally be āhārīkṛta, 'made into food, consumed'; with the short a printed it mirrors the song's spelling rather than interpreting it. The context fits both: 'lost in the ocean of clear light' and 'made my own, eaten, through unbroken practice'. So Munidatta's wording here (cp.35.m5) does not decide between 'lost' and 'ate'. I render 'lost', with the song draft.

lakṣyam iti bhāvyam uktaṃ could also mean '"the mark" is said to be what is to be meditated on', with uktam as the gloss-marker. I take uktam as rendering the song's bhaṇiā ('having spoken'), pradattam its dila ('gave') and mahyam its 'to me'. The daṇḍa after sādaranirantarābhyāsena interrupts one clause (mayā ... ahārīkṛtam) into which the gloss on 'sky' is inserted.
The folio mark [৫২] (52) inside the segment, after bājuletyādi, is Shastri's note of the manuscript folio; it is kept in the transliteration and not translated.

segments.translit:
caturthapādenātmasvarūpam āha—
bhaṇai ityādi| abhāga iti| anutpādabhāgagṛhīto 'ha[ṃ] bhadrapādaḥ| yad anādibhavavikalpādhāracittarājo mayā sarvvadharmmānupalambhasamudre praveśitaṃ| 35|
segments.translation: With the fourth [verse]{pada} he states his own [true nature]{svarupa}. 'Says', and so on. '[Abhāga]{abhaga}' means: I, [Bhadrapāda]{p-bhadra}, who have taken the share of [non-arising]{anutpada}. For I have made the [king of mind]{king-of-mind}, the support of the [conceptual thoughts]{vikalpa} of beginningless [existence]{bhava}, enter the [ocean]{ocean} of the [non-apprehension]{anupalambha} of all [dharmas]{dharma}. (35)
segments.note: Munidatta reads [abhāga]{abhaga} ('without a share') as the share of [non-arising]{anutpada}, which [Bhadrapāda]{p-bhadra} has taken: he has made the [king of mind]{king-of-mind}, support of the [conceptual thoughts]{vikalpa} of beginningless existence, enter the [ocean]{ocean} of the [non-apprehension]{anupalambha} of all [dharmas]{dharma} (cp.35.m6). The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) agrees, rendering the poet's name bzang po'i zhabs.

equations.en: the share of non-arising (anutpādabhāga), which Bhadrapāda has taken

flags.note: anutpādabhāgagṛhītaḥ: I translate 'who have taken the share of non-arising', with the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) (ma skyes pa'i cha bzang po'i zhabs bdag gis blangs pa, 'I, Bhadrapāda, have taken the share of the unborn'). As a compound it could also mean 'seized by the share of non-arising'. Munidatta does not say how abhāga yields this (cp.35.m6); perhaps he takes bhāga as 'share' and the a- as the syllable a, a familiar emblem of non-arising, but that is my inference, not his statement.

Munidatta's paraphrase of 5b (cp.35.m6: 'I have made the king of mind enter the ocean of non-apprehension', praveśitam) uses neither 'lose' nor 'eat' for ahāra kaelā. Sinking into an ocean sits closer to 'lost' than to 'ate', but it does not decide. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293)'s verse line 5b has stor bar gyur ('was lost'), as in 4b.

yad stands beside the masculine cittarājaḥ; I take it as a conjunction ('for, in that'), explaining 5b. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) treats it as a relative (gang ..., 'the king of mind which ...') and has rab tu zhugs pa ('entered') for the causative praveśitam ('made to enter').

[ṃ] in gṛhīto 'ha[ṃ] is Shastri's restoration. The final 35 is the song number, given in parentheses. Munidatta here (cp.35.m6) writes caturthapāda (long ā) for his usual caturthapada; I translate it 'fourth verse' as elsewhere.

questions: 4a, who gives the mark: Munidatta's 'vajrakuleneti| vajraguruṇā' (cp.35.m5) is a gloss in his 'X iti Y' form. It makes the vajrakula the agent (instrumental) of 'spoke and gave', and identifies it with the vajra guru. He gives no personal name. The Tibetan verse line's Rāhula (rA hu la yis) gets no support from his Sanskrit, and the Tibetan comment itself glosses its rA hu la as rdo rje'i rigs. That supports the draft's 'The vajrakula' as the subject of 4a. Should 4a carry a note saying that Munidatta takes the vajrakula as the vajra guru (cp.35.m5) and that the Tibetan line names Rāhula? And is 'vajrakula' meant as a title (capitalized, 'the Vajrakula') or as a common noun?

4b and 5b, ahār-: Munidatta does not decide between 'lost' and 'ate'. His ahārīkṛtam (cp.35.m5) is the song's own word put into Sanskrit form; taken strictly as Sanskrit (āhārīkṛta) it would lean to 'made into food', but the short a mirrors the song. His paraphrase of 5b, praveśitam, 'made to enter the ocean' (cp.35.m6), uses neither sense. The Tibetan verse lines have stor ('was lost') in both, and the comment's ster in cp.35.m5 is probably a slip for stor. I kept 'lost' in the commentary translation. If you switch the song to 'ate' / 'made a meal of', m5's 'lost it' should change with it.

m2 (cp.35.m2), kalyāṇamitrasaṃsargāt: I translate as printed ('from association with a spiritual friend'), reading it as a compressed advance paraphrase of 1b. Would you rather emend to 'for lack of association' (°mitrāsaṃsargāt), which reads more smoothly but has no support from the Tibetan?

3b: should the song draft carry a witness note that, in Munidatta's comment on this line (cp.35.m4), the Tibetan has bzhi pa shar bas ('through the dawning of the fourth') where the Sanskrit has cittasyānudayena ('through the non-arising of mind')?

m4 (cp.35.m4): is the coordinate reading ('I know sin and merit and the like, and the bond of saṃsāra') acceptable? Or do you prefer the predicative one ('I know sin, merit and the like to be the bond of saṃsāra'), which the Tibetan follows?
m5: "fourth joy" is marked as fourth [joy]{ananda}, as in songs 1, 13 and 16. Should caturthānanda have its own glossary entry (it recurs in Munidatta), moving the form চতুর্থানন্দ out of "joy"?

5a abhāga: Munidatta (cp.35.m6) does not say how abhāga becomes 'the share of non-arising'. I suggest in a flag that he may take the a- as the syllable a, emblem of non-arising. Is that worth a note, or too speculative?
